content.thinking:
I'm starting with the symptom: account pages were loading slowly, though nothing was failing. Next I'm working through a causal chain, starting with the idea that shoppers saw slow account pages and median latency went up. I'm weighing whether the ClientDisconnected entries in the logs could explain it, since shoppers may have closed their connections, but I can't yet tell if those were already present before the 01:36–01:43 window.

I'm now checking why the cache lookups were refused. The deploy changed the cache port from 6379 to 6380, and the connection failures happen at 6380, while the service rendered normally before that change.

I'm now ruling out the earlier deploy: the metrics I read cover the period after it, and they stay at baseline until the onset at 01:37, and the account page rendered normally with that earlier change in place. The only other flag change came from the rollback I confirmed, which just restored the port. That leaves the cache port change as the candidate, since the service was healthy at 6379 and connections to 6380 are refused.

I'm checking the causal chain against the record: account pages are slow for shoppers, and the lookups that should serve the cached summary are being refused at port 6380 instead of the 6379 the service used before. The deploy changed that port, and nothing accepting connections there means every lookup falls back to the slower recompute path.

I'm noting the log lookups were refused for most requests, peaking at 01:37, which fits the 01:36 start. The deploy's port change is the step I'm checking now, and I'm working through why the new port failed while the old one served normally.

I'm settling on the cause in plain terms: the deploy pointed account pages at a cache address where nothing accepted connections, so each page recomputed its spend figure from scratch, which stayed correct but slow. The mechanism rests only on readings already checked, so I'm treating it as a real cause, with the repository still holding the changed port as the open item.

I'm settling on what the repository still says: the cache port the lookups were refused on is still held there, so if automatic sync goes back on before a fix is merged, the slowdown could come straight back. Next I'm turning to the contributing factors, starting with whether anyone checked that the configured cache address accepted connections before the deploy went out.

I'm listing contributing factors now: the change went out without anyone checking that the configured cache address accepted connections, and no readiness check tested cache connectivity, which could have halted the rollout.

I'm weighing the remaining contributing factors: the missing readiness check for cache connectivity let new replicas take traffic they couldn't serve properly, and I'm setting aside the paging gap for the went-wrong list instead of treating it as a factor that would have shortened the incident.

I'm drafting the action items now, starting with a pre-deploy check that the cache host and port accept connections before a release goes out. I'm also weighing a startup check that halts the io-shop rollout when new replicas can't reach the summary cache, and I'm considering an alert on cache connection failures so the problem surfaces sooner than the latency alert did.

I'm picking up the post-incident review now: the investigator's onset timing and the rollback, confirmation, and draft fix all went as planned, along with the flag-history check that ruled out other changes. The remaining item is the paging gap, which I'm noting for the went-wrong list.

I'm checking the remaining sections of the review: nobody was paged, and that's the only gap I'm noting. The fault was a deliberate configuration choice, so leaving automatic sync off is by design, and the incident's cause is settled. The main thing left is the assumption that the cache was listening on its previous port, which I'm inferring from normal renders before the change and recovery after the rollback rather than measuring directly.

I'm ruling out the earlier deploy again: metrics from before the onset show the service healthy with that revision in place, and account pages rendered normally in the minutes before 01:37. Rolling back to it also restored service, and no feature-flag changes came from anyone but Argus in the hour before. The source code side looks unchanged, since the only file the deploy touched was the production values file.

I'm settling the wording of the cache-port sentence, then writing up the remaining report sections: the rolled-out date, how the latency series is measured, and the went-well entries, each tied to the actor who did it.

action_items.item: Add a pre-deploy check that the summary cache host and port in deploy/values-production.yaml accept connections in the production cluster, and block the deploy if they do not.
Make io-shop's rollout stop when new replicas cannot connect to the summary cache at startup, leaving the previous revision serving.
Add an alert on io-shop's summary cache lookup failures (refused connections) and cache hit ratio.
Link the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly. The typical (median) time io-shop took to answer a request rose well above its usual level and stayed there, while no more requests failed than usual.
Account pages could not use the rendered-summary cache. Every lookup to it was refused, so the page fell back to working each shopper's spend figure out again on each request, which is the slow path.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy P1 of revision 544cef3: metrics read back over the hours before the onset show the service healthy with it in place until the onset, and rolling back to it put the service back to normal.
A feature flag change: the flag provider's history showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before.
A change to io-shop's source code: the deploy's diff changes only deploy/values-production.yaml.

causal_chain.step: The lookups went to a new cache port. Deploy P2 at {P2.1} changed the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2} and changed nothing else. As of {T11.1}, all {T11.2} replicas were running that revision.
The change broke the service because nothing accepted connections on the new port, while the old port had served account pages normally.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A configuration change pointed the shop's account pages at an address where their cache could not be reached, so every page had to work its figures out from scratch, which kept the pages correct but made them slow.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen, in review or before the deploy, that the cache address in the deployment configuration accepts connections in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The port change would have been caught before it reached production, and account pages would not have slowed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen during the rollout that new replicas could reach the summary cache, so all replicas moved to the revision that could not reach it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The rollout would have stopped with the previous revision still serving, and the slowdown would have been held back or cut short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No alert on refused summary cache lookups was seen. The fault was found only by the latency alert, whose rule waits with its condition holding before it fires.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The refused lookups, logged from the minute of the deploy, could have raised an alert sooner, and the rollback would have come sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read the diff of the deploy running on every replica and found the cache port change.
Argus checked the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone but itself.
The Mitigation Agent rolled io-shop back off revision 0d8e826.
The Mitigation Agent saw that the service was no longer at the incident's level and judged the rollback confirmed.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix to the deployment configuration as draft pull request #566.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was linked to no on-call incident, so no person was brought in while production was slow.

input.root_cause: Deploy 0d8e826 changed the summary cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}. Nothing on the cache host accepted connections on the new port, so every cache lookup was refused. The account page handles an unreachable cache by working each shopper's spend figure out again from scratch, so pages stayed correct but became slow.
input.still_at_risk: The repository still sets the cache port that refused every lookup, so syncing the repository back into production before a fix is merged could slow account pages again.
